anomaly_def.Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled allocation of buffer caches, plan caches, per-query work areas, and background heaps pushes the database process beyond the safe physical-memory envelope, provoking paging, OOM terminations, or node eviction.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures on disk become internally inconsistent—broken page links, checksum failures, or incorrect key ordering—so that persisted data can no longer be trusted.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space for data files, logs, archives, or temporary areas approaches zero, causing allocation failures, stalled checkpoints, and inability to persist further changes.

When these three root causes manifest concurrently, the system can exhibit a rapidly deteriorating health profile:  • Memory pressure forces hash, sort, and spill operations to disk, but the same disk is near capacity, so temporary-file growth quickly consumes the last free blocks.  • Impending space exhaustion prevents checkpoints, log switches, or index rebuilds from completing, increasing the volume of dirty or inconsistent pages.  • Corrupted pages encountered during IO retries or after forced restarts trigger repeated read faults; each retry amplifies memory churn and fills error logs until the logging destination itself runs out of space.  • Queries that would normally use indexes fall back to full scans because of corruption, inflating buffer-cache turnover and temporary-space consumption, further intensifying both memory and space pressure.  • Administrators observe a mixture of OOM kills, "no space left on device" errors, checksum or page-corruption reports, and sudden performance collapse, making root-cause isolation difficult as symptoms overlap and propagate across resource boundaries.

Causally, tight memory amplifies disk-space usage by pushing intermediate data to temp areas; dwindling space, in turn, forces aggressive cache eviction and limits log growth, provoking additional memory allocations for recovery and error handling. Repeated abrupt terminations from OOM or failed writes interrupt clean shutdown paths, heightening the chance of incomplete page flushes and thereby seeding further block or index corruption. Once corruption exists, the optimizer may abandon indexes, increasing workload intensity on both memory and storage. The intertwined feedback loops—memory overcommitment triggering spills, spills accelerating space exhaustion, and space or power-loss related write failures corrupting pages that then inflate memory and temp demand—cause a compounding degradation that can culminate in systemic unavailability or data loss unless all three dimensions are simultaneously mitigated.

entry.official_definition: Aborts any statement that takes more than the specified amount of time; zero disables the timeout.
entry.trigger_condition: A SQL statement runs longer than statement_timeout, measured from command arrival until completion.
entry.workload_impact: The running statement is aborted; when configured, the timed-out statement is logged.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when statement execution exceeds a configured execution-time budget because the operation runs too long or the workload is blocked behind other work.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect query shape, access path quality, resource contention, and whether the timeout threshold should be reviewed together with the workload pattern.
